newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Strikes no cause to slow labour reforms - minister.
newsitem.headline: Strikes no cause to slow labour reforms - minister.

text.p: South Korea, viewed with increasing wariness by investors concerned about chronic worker unrest, will press ahead with labour reforms that have sparked crippling strikes, Labour Minister Jin Nyum said on Friday.
At a news conference, Jin dismissed condemnation of South Korea's new labour legislation by the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU) as biased.
He said the new law, allowing troubled companies to lay off employees and hire temporary workers to replace striking union members, would give flexibility to the labour market.

"There is no country in the world except Korea where wages have increased by an annual average of 15 percent, or eight percent when price hikes are considered, in the past 10 years. And yet violent labour strife is an annual affair," he said.
"You can't help but ask whether you could continue economic activities under these circumstances," he said.
Jin said unionists demanding better conditions had often turned workplaces into battlegrounds to disrupt production in the past decade, forcing losses on helpless management.

He said rapid wage increases were a major factor hampering the country's economic competitiveness. The average wage for manufacturing workers was 1.7 times per capita income in South Korea against 1.2 times in the United States or Japan, he said.

"Many businessmen complain it is difficult to do business in South Korea, and set up plants in Wales, Scotland and other foreign countries," he added. "There is no customer in the world who wants to buy products out of plants where petrol bombs fly because of violent labour disputes."
But Jin rejected allegations by the Brussels-based ICFTU that the new legislation was a step backward for workers. "There is nothing in the new law that worsens the rights of workers," he said.

He noted that the new law allowed unions to be involved in political activity, removed provisions barring outside intervention in labour disputes and opened the way for multiple union representation from 2002.

"The ICFTU is only looking at one side of the issue, focusing on civil servants and teachers. People from the American Chamber of Commerce and investors in Korea complain about the rigid labour market," he said.
Civil servants and teachers will remain barred from forming labour unions.

The outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions was due to be legalised under earlier drafts of the law, but when the ruling New Korea Party rammed it through parliament on December 26 recognition was delayed until 2000.

The move enraged the union body which organised nationwide strikes. The confederation, which claims half a million members, said about 190,000 workers were on strike but the labour ministry put the figure at 70,000.
Asked if the legislation could have been delayed in view of protests by workers and opposition deputies, Jin said:
"The current economic reality is too urgent and serious for us to delay the decision."
Jin acknowledged the new law did not fully conform with the standards and practices of the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development that Seoul has just joined.
"The law cannot be elevated to that of the OECD overnight, but it is great progress for the better."
